Its interpretation is either, according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas in explaining His words, ﴿they distort words from their places﴾ [al-Nisa': 46], that it is distortion through misunderstanding and not alteration of the Torah's wording; or its interpretation is that the distortion occurred after the descent of this surah, when the Muhammadan call became apparent and the passages of the Torah indicating the attributes of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) confronted the Jews; or its interpretation is that the oath is by what it contains of true revelation.

"And by the frequented House": on the authority of al-Hasan, it is the Ka'bah, and this is the most fitting given its conjunction with the Tur,

and its description as ﴿frequented﴾, because it is never without someone circumambulating it, and the populating of the Ka'bah is its populating by those who circumambulate it. He, exalted is He, said ﴿Only those populate the mosques of God who believe in God and the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18], etc.

And its descent was a law abrogating the law of the Torah. Moreover, revelation used to descend around the Ka'bah. The relevance of the oath by it is that Fir'awn and his people were destroyed in it when Musa and the Children of Israel entered it, and Fir'awn followed them.

"Al-Masjur": it is said to mean "filled", derived from sajr, which is filling and supplying. It is then a clarifying descriptor, intended to remind of the state in which God created it, filled with water without valleys or torrents filling it, or it is to exclude the meaning of a valley, since a valley diminishes and does not remain full; and this indicates the greatness of power. My preferred view is that describing it as "kindled" is an allusion to

the state in which Fir'awn was destroyed after God parted the sea for Musa and the Children of Israel and then kindled it, i.e., poured it over Fir'awn and his chiefs.

Al-Daf': removing a thing from another by the hand, and it is here applied metaphorically to protection, by the relation of

the generalisation that none of them would be shielded from God's punishment by intercession or opposition.

In another narration: "So I embraced Islam, out of fear of the descent of the punishment, and I did not think I would move from my place before the punishment befell me."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verses 13–16:

Page 43
﴿On the Day they will be pushed violently into the Fire of Hell.﴾ ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Is this magic, or is it that you do not see?﴾ ﴿Burn therein; then whether you bear it patiently or not, it is all the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾

﴿يَوْمَ يُدَعُّونَ﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿يَوْمَ تَمُورُ السَّماءُ مَوْرًا﴾ [al-Tur: 9], and it is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of a part that includes the whole sense).

Al-da‘ (الدَّعُّ) means forceful pushing, and that is a humiliation of them and harshness toward them. That is, on the Day they will be driven toward the Fire of Hell with violent driving. Within it is a depiction of their state: they are frightened and recoiling, so the angels appointed to drive them push them toward the Fire.

The emphasis of يُدَعُّونَ with ﴿دَعًّا﴾ serves to convey its magnitude through its indefiniteness.

The clause ﴿هَذِهِ النّارُ﴾ to its end is a statement (maqul) of a deleted saying, indicated by the context. The deleted saying may be estimated as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿يُدَعُّونَ﴾. Its estimate is: "It will be said to them," or "as something said to them," and the speakers are the angels appointed to bring them to Hell.

The demonstrative ﴿هَذِهِ﴾, which is for a near feminine referent, indicates that they reach it while standing on its edge. The purpose of the demonstrative is to prepare for what follows it, from ﴿الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ بِها تُكَذِّبُونَ﴾ to ﴿لا تُبْصِرُونَ﴾.

The relative pronoun and its relative clause in ﴿الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ بِها تُكَذِّبُونَ﴾ serve to alert the addressees to the corruption of their opinion, since they denied the Gathering and the punishment and now see it directly.

Following this alert, another alert is given concerning their misguidance in the world, through ﴿أفَسِحْرٌ هَذا﴾, since when they heard the warning of the Day of Resurrection and recompense they would say, "This is magic," and when the Qur'an was presented to them they said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾ [Fussilat: 5]. So, because of the correspondence between what is in the relative clause, the meaning of reproach for their error, and the mockery directed at them through what they used to say, the resumptive fa' (فاء التفريع) entered, and this is among what is said to them, reported by the estimated saying.

Page 44
The ﴿أمْ﴾ is disjunctive (munqati‘ah), and the interrogation that ﴿أمْ﴾ requires after it is used for rebuke and mockery. The estimate is: "Rather, you do not see."
The meaning of ﴿لا تُبْصِرُونَ﴾ is: you do not see visible things as they really are. Perhaps you claim that you do not see a fire, as you used to say in the world: ﴿Between us and you is a barrier﴾ [Fussilat: 5], meaning, "we do not see you," and you say ﴿Our sight has only been intoxicated﴾ [al-Hijr: 15].

The predicate is given in the form of a verbal sentence, after the subject is stated first, to convey the strengthening of the judgment. For this reason it does not say ﴿أمْ لا تُبْصِرُونَ﴾, because that does not convey strengthening; nor ﴿أمْ لا تُبْصِرُونَ أنْتُمْ﴾, because the coming of the separate pronoun after the attached pronoun conveys the affirmation of the subject about which the judgment is made, unlike the fronting of the subject, which conveys the emphasis and strengthening of the judgment and is stronger in emphasis. All of this is in the manner of mockery.

The clause ﴿اصْلَوْها﴾ is a resumed (mustanif) clause, which stands in the position of the expected result of the preceding rebuke and harshness. That is: enter it and warm yourselves by its fire. One says ṣalā al-nār (صَلِيَ النّارَ), yaṣlāhā, when one endures its heat.

The imperative in ﴿اصْلَوْها﴾ is either a metonymy for entering, because entering it necessarily entails being burned by its fire, or it is used figuratively for punishment. Following ﴿اصْلَوْها﴾ comes an imperative of equalization between their patience under its heat and their non-patience, which is anguish, because neither of the two lightens any part of the punishment for them. Do you not see that they say: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we show anguish or patience; we have no escape﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]? Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verses 17–19:

﴿Indeed, the God-conscious will be in gardens and bliss,﴾ ﴿enjoying what their Lord has given them, and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do."﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) after mention of the state of the deniers and what is said to them. It is natural for the listener to ask about the condition of their opposites, namely the group who affirmed the Messenger (ﷺ) and what the Qur'an brought, especially since the listeners were believers. The Qur'an's custom is to follow warning with good news and vice versa. The sentence is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between what precedes it and the clause ﴿Or do they say, "He is a poet"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30].

The emphasis of the report with "inna" (indeed) is for giving it importance. The indefiniteness of ﴿gardens and bliss﴾ is for magnification, meaning: in what gardens and what bliss.

The plural "jannat" (gardens) has already been discussed in surah al-Dhariyat.

Al-fakih (enjoying) is a descriptive form from fakiha, like fariha, meaning that one's soul becomes content and pleased.

The majority read "fakihin" in the form of the active participle, while Abu Ja'far read "fakihin" without the alif.

The "ba'" in ﴿for what their Lord has given them﴾ indicates cause, and the meaning is that their Lord pleased them with what they love.

Mentioning the Majesty by describing "their Lord" points to the greatness of what He has given them, since giving corresponds to the state of the giver. Adding "Lord" to their pronoun brings Him near to them and magnifies Him. The clause ﴿and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with the waw being circumstantial, or conjunctive with "muttaki'in" which is a circumstance; the estimate is: "and indeed their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire," and it is a circumstance of the God-conscious. The purpose of mentioning this state is to show the contrast between the state of the God-conscious and the state of the deniers, increasing the favor, for blessing becomes more pleasant to the soul when its opposite is observed.

Also in it: their protection from the punishment of the Blazing Fire is justice, since they had not committed what necessitates punishment. As for what they were given of bliss, that is grace from God and His honoring of them.

In His saying "their Lord" is what preceded just before it.

The clause ﴿Eat and drink﴾ to its end is a quoted speech of an omitted saying, also in the position of a circumstance, its estimate being: "It is said to them," or "said to them." This saying is the counterpart of what is said to the deniers: ﴿Burn therein; so be patient or be not patient; it is all the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ [al-Tur: 16].

The omission of the object of ﴿Eat and drink﴾ is for conveying bliss, meaning: eat whatever is eaten and drink every drink, a customary generality, i.e., of what you desire.

"Hani'an" is a noun on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, used as a descriptor of two verbal nouns for the verbs ﴿eat and drink﴾, eating and drinking; therefore the adjective is not feminized, because fa'il in the sense of maf'ul requires singular and masculine. It was discussed in surah al-Nisa', because it is free of what troubles food and drink.

"Ma" is a relative pronoun, and the "ba'" is causal, meaning: because of the righteous deed which his words "the God-conscious" allude to. In this statement there is an increase of honor for them by showing that what they were given of honor is a recompense for their deeds, as the causal "ba'" indicates. It is like the words of one who bestows a favor upon the one he benefits: "I have no favor over you, it is only your own property," or something similar.

It is natural for the listener to ask about the condition of their opposites, namely the group who affirmed the Messenger (ﷺ) and what the Qur'an brought, especially since the listeners were believers. The Qur'an's custom is to follow warning with good news and vice versa. The sentence is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between what precedes it and the clause ﴿Or do they say, "He is a poet"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30].

The emphasis of the report with "inna" (indeed) is for giving it importance. The indefiniteness of ﴿gardens and bliss﴾ is for magnification, meaning: in what gardens and what bliss.

The plural "jannat" (gardens) has already been discussed in surah al-Dhariyat.

Al-fakih (enjoying) is a descriptive form from fakiha, like fariha, meaning that one's soul becomes content and pleased.

The majority read "fakihin" in the form of the active participle, while Abu Ja'far read "fakihin" without the alif.

The "ba'" in ﴿for what their Lord has given them﴾ indicates cause, and the meaning is that their Lord pleased them with what they love.

Mentioning the Majesty by describing "their Lord" points to the greatness of what He has given them, since giving corresponds to the state of the giver. Adding "Lord" to their pronoun brings Him near to them and magnifies Him. The clause ﴿and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with the waw being circumstantial, or conjunctive with "muttaki'in" which is a circumstance; the estimate is: "and indeed their Lord has protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire," and it is a circumstance of the God-conscious. The purpose of mentioning this state is to show the contrast between the state of the God-conscious and the state of the deniers, increasing the favor, for blessing becomes more pleasant to the soul when its opposite is observed.

Also in it: their protection from the punishment of the Blazing Fire is justice, since they had not committed what necessitates punishment. As for what they were given of bliss, that is grace from God and His honoring of them.

In His saying "their Lord" is what preceded just before it.

The clause ﴿Eat and drink﴾ to its end is a quoted speech of an omitted saying, also in the position of a circumstance, its estimate being: "It is said to them," or "said to them." This saying is the counterpart of what is said to the deniers: ﴿Burn therein; so be patient or be not patient; it is all the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ [al-Tur: 16].

The omission of the object of ﴿Eat and drink﴾ is for conveying bliss, meaning: eat whatever is eaten and drink every drink, a customary generality, i.e., of what you desire.

"Hani'an" is a noun on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, used as a descriptor of two verbal nouns for the verbs ﴿eat and drink﴾, eating and drinking; therefore the adjective is not feminized, because fa'il in the sense of maf'ul requires singular and masculine. It was discussed in surah al-Nisa', because it is free of what troubles food and drink.

"Ma" is a relative pronoun, and the "ba'" is causal, meaning: because of the righteous deed which his words "the God-conscious" allude to. In this statement there is an increase of honor for them by showing that what they were given of honor is a recompense for their deeds, as the causal "ba'" indicates. It is like the words of one who bestows a favor upon the one he benefits: "I have no favor over you, it is only your own property," or something similar.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 20:

﴿Reclining on couches arranged in rows, and We shall wed them to huris with large, lovely eyes.﴾

This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿Eat and drink﴾ [al-Tur: 19]. That is, it is said to them, "Eat and drink," while they are reclining, meaning that they are in the manner of eating familiar among the people of luxury in this world. People of ease used to eat while reclining, and the Qur'an described this in Surah Yusuf with His words: ﴿She sent for them and prepared for them a banquet (mutaka'), and gave each one of them a knife﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. The Chosroes (al-Akasira) and the marzabans (marazbah) of the Persians used to eat while reclining, and likewise the emperors (abatira) of the Romans; and their custom in drinking wine was the same. Al-A'sha said:

I contended with them, reclining, over sprigs of basil, and over a sharp wine whose strainer is moist.

Al-Sururu (the couches) is the plural of sarir, which is that upon which one lies down.

Al-Mastufah means "facing one another," and the meaning is that they eat reclining, gathered together for companionship, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿on couches facing one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 44].

The clause "wa zawwajnahum" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "muttaki'in," so it is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

The meaning of "zawwajnahum" is: We made each one of them a spouse (zawj), i.e., not single, that is, We paired them with huris with large, lovely eyes. The bāʾ (ba') here indicates accompaniment, i.e., We made huris to be with them. The verb "zawwajnahum" was not transitive to "ḥūr" directly as an object, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿We gave her to you in marriage﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]; because "zawwajna" in this verse does not mean "ankahnahum" (we married them), since the intended meaning is not the contract of marriage, as this meaning is far from the intent. So "tazwij" here is used in its literal linguistic sense, which is making a single thing a spouse, and not in the sense it carries in common usage or in the Shariah. The bāʾ is not there to make "zawwajnahum" transitive by implying the meaning of "qaranā" (We joined them), nor is it according to the dialect of the Azd Shanu'ah, for it has not been heard in eloquent speech: "tazawwaja bi-imra'ah" (he married a woman).

"Ḥūr" is an attribute of the wives of the believers in Paradise, and they are the women who were their spouses in this world if they were believing women, and whom Allah creates in Paradise as a blessing of Paradise. The ruling on the wives of believers who are themselves believers but did not have righteous deeds like their husbands, concerning their joining their husbands in ranks in Paradise, was explained at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, delighted﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 70] in Surat al-Zukhruf; and what is said of them is said of the men who are spouses of righteous women.

"ʿIn" is a second attribute, and its proper form would be to be conjoined (by ʿaṭf), but omitting the conjunction has become common.

"Who believed, and whose offspring followed them in faith — We shall join their offspring with them, and We shall not deprive them of anything of their deeds. Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned."

This is a parenthetical digression (i'tiraḍ) between the mention of the honours of the believers, and the waw is a waw of parenthesis (waw i'tirāḍiyya).

The use of the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) here is a manifestation in the place of a pronoun (iẓhār fī maqām al-iḍmār), so that the relative clause (ṣila) serves as an indication (īmā') of the reason for the construction of the predicate that follows it. That is: the cause of the joining of their offspring with them in the bliss of Paradise is their own faith, and the offspring having believed because of the faith of their fathers; for believing fathers instil faith in their children.

The meaning: "And the believers who have offspring who are believers — We shall join their offspring with them."

Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 6]. Can any one of you protect the Fire from another except through guidance? Perhaps what is in the verse, of joining their offspring, is from the intercession of the righteous believer for his family and his descendants.

The indefiniteness in His words "bi-īmānin" (with a faith) may be for magnification (li-l-ta'ẓīm), that is: with a great faith, and its greatness is by the abundance of righteous deeds; so that would be a condition for their being joined to their fathers, and the blessing would be in placing them in one place.

It may also be for the sense of kind (li-l-nawʿiyya), that is: with whatever truly qualifies as faith.

Al-Jumhūr read "wa-ittaba'athum" with a hamzat waṣl and with a doubled first tā', and with a tā' after the 'ayn, which is the feminine tā' of the verb's pronoun. Abū 'Amr alone read "wa-atba'nāhum" with a hamzat qaṭ' and a sukūn on the tā'.

His words "dhurriyyatuhum" (first occurrence): al-Jumhūr read it in the singular form. Abū 'Amr read "dhurriyyātihim" in the plural form of dhurriyya, so it is the object of "atba'nāhum." Ibn 'Āmir and Ya'qūb read it also in the plural but in the nominative, as the subject of "ittaba'athum," so the favour is bestowed upon their fathers by joining their offspring to them even if they did not do the same deeds as theirs.

A group of scholars, including al-Ṭabarī, al-Bazzār, Ibn 'Adī, Abū Nu'aym and Ibn Mardawayh, narrated a hadith with a chain going back to Ibn 'Abbās, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Allah raises the offspring of the believer to his rank, even if they are below him," that is, in deeds, as stated in the narration of al-Qurṭubī: "so that his eye may be gladdened by them." Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾ up to His words ﴿of anything﴾.

On both possibilities, it is a blessing by which Allah gathers for the believers all kinds of joy: by their happiness in being paired with the ḥūr (maidens), by the companionship of believing brothers, and by the gathering of their children and descendants with them. This is because it is in human nature to be fond of his children and to love their being connected to him.

Muḥammad ibn 'Abd al-Raf'īʿ al-Ja'farī al-Mursī al-Andalusī, a resident of Tunis in the year 1013 AH, described this in a book he named "al-Anwār al-Nabawiyya fī Ābā' Khayr al-Bariyya" (The Prophetic Lights concerning the Fathers of the Best of Creation). He said at the end of the book: "Allah the Exalted has made me aware of the religion of Islam through my father when I was six years old, although at that time I used to go to the school of the Christians to learn their religion, then return to my house, where my father would teach me the religion of Islam, so I used to learn both together (thus) — and my age when I was taken to their school was four years. My father took a tablet of walnut wood, as if I see it now, smooth, without ṭafl (a name for dry clay, which is sticky clay and is not Arabic; its Arabic form is ṭufāl, like ghurāb), and he wrote for me the letters of the alphabet, and asked me about the letters of the Christians, letter by letter, in training and in approximation. When I named a foreign letter to him, he would write for me an Arabic letter, until he had completed all the letters of the alphabet. He instructed me to keep this secret even from my mother, my uncle and my brother, although he — may Allah have mercy on him — had put himself in danger of destruction, since I might have reported this about him and he would inevitably have been burned. He used to teach me what to say when I saw the idols. When my father realised that I was concealing the matters of the religion of Islam, he commanded me to speak openly of it to my mother and to some of his friends. I travelled from Jaén to meet the righteous Muslims in Granada, Seville, Toledo and other cities of the Green Peninsula, and from my acquaintance with them it became clear to me that I had distinguished seven men who used to tell me about the conditions of Granada and what was there of Islam; and they all passed by a shaykh of the shaykhs of Granada called al-Faqīh al-Awṭūrī..." etc.

The choice of the verb "alḥaqnā" (We joined), rather than saying "adkhalnā ma'ahum" (We made them enter with them) or "ja'alnā ma'ahum" (We made them with them), is because of what the meaning of joining includes of eligibility for success and of delay. It may be that this joining comes after a punishment has been executed on some of the offspring, which they deserved because of their evil deeds, given the variation among deeds in the deservingness of punishment; and Allah knows best His intention regarding His servants. The verb of joining implies that the offspring become in the ranks of their fathers.

In the variation between the two forms there is an artistic variety (tafannun) to avoid repeating the same word.

"Alatnāhum" means "We diminished them." It is said: "ālahu ḥaqqahu," when he diminished it for him, and it is of the pattern ḍaraba and of the pattern 'alima.

Al-Jumhūr read "alatnāhum" with a fatḥa on the lām. Ibn Kathīr read it with a kasra on the lām ("ilitnāhum"), and this was discussed earlier at His words ﴿He will not deprive you of anything of your deeds﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 14] in Surat al-Ḥujurāt.

The waw is for the circumstantial (li-l-ḥāl), and the pronoun of the third person refers to "alladhīna āmanū."

The meaning: Allah joined their offspring with them in rank in Paradise, as a favour from Him to those who believed, without any compensation, lest they suppose that the joining of their offspring with them comes after giving some of their good deeds to their offspring so that they may enter Paradise by them, according to what is customary among them in ransoming a captive, bearing blood-money, and freeing debtors; and according to what is known in taking retribution from the wrongdoer for the wronged, by taking from the wrongdoer's good deeds and giving them to the wronged. This is a kinaya for the non-reduction of their shares of reward for righteous deeds.

"Min 'amalihim" is connected to "mā alatnāhum," and "min" is partitive, and the "min" in His words "min shay'" is for emphasizing the negation and for conveying the comprehensiveness and totality of the indefinite.

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾.

This is a parenthetical clause between the clause "﴿and We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾" and the clause "﴿and We provided them with fruit﴾" [al-Ṭūr: 22]. It is intended to give the reason for the preceding clause, and by its generality it is suitable both as a conclusion (tadhyīl) and as a reason (ta'līl). "Kullu impi'in" includes all the people of the Hereafter.

The intended meaning is not "every person from among the God-fearing" specifically.

The meaning: the reduction by Us of anything of their deeds is negated; because every person is bound to what he has earned and held in pledge by it, and the God-fearing, since they earned righteous deeds, have them as a necessary companion, attached to them; they are not stripped of any of it. What is meant by "what they earned" is the reward of what they earned, because that is what attaches to the doer of the deed; as for the deed itself, it has passed in its time.

In this reasoning there are two kinayas: first, that the people of disbelief are attached to the recompense of their deeds; and second, that the offspring of the believers who were joined with their fathers in bliss were joined to Paradise out of honour to their fathers; and had it not been for that honour, their treatment would have been according to their deeds. For this reason this clause has a more beautiful effect than anything else, and it has become one of the most beautiful completions (ḥusn al-tatmīm).

Al-kasb is applied to what a person obtains by his action with the intention of benefiting himself.

Rahīn: a form of fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl, from al-rahn, which is confinement (al-ḥabs).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verses 22–23:

﴿And We provided them with fruit and meat, of whatever they desire.﴾ ﴿They pass around among themselves a cup, free of idle talk and sinful conduct.﴾ This is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) on ﴿in gardens and bliss﴾ [al-Tur: 17], etc.

Page 52
Al-imdād (provision) is giving madad (increase), which is an addition of a beneficial kind in that to which it is added. That is: We increased them, beyond what was mentioned of bliss, eating and wholesome drinking, with fruit and meat of whatever they desire, of the fruits and meats that they long for. That is: nothing is brought to them that they do not desire, so each of them has whatever he wishes.

He singled out fruit and meat as a preparation (tamhīd) for His saying, ﴿They pass around among themselves a cup, free of idle talk and sinful conduct.﴾ God granted them in the Hereafter the pleasure of the intoxication of wine and of companionship over drinking it, because it is among the finest pleasures to which their souls are accustomed. And the people of luxury in this world, when they drank wine in this world, would break its fierceness in the belly with roasted meat. Al-Nabigha said, describing the horn of a bull:

"A drinking-skewer they forgot at the time of its heat..."

And they would ward off the sting of wine from their mouths by eating fruits, and they called them al-nuql (pronounced with a damma or a fatḥa on the nūn), and these may be from fruits and melons.

For this reason His saying ﴿they pass around﴾ is brought as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of absence in ﴿We provided them with fruit﴾, etc.

The verb tanāzaʿa was applied to taking turns and passing things to one another. Its origin is a reciprocal form (tafāʿul) from nazʿ al-dalw min al-bi'r (drawing the bucket from the well) when drawing water: when people came to draw water, one of them would pull his bucket from the water, then hand the bucket to those around him; and often a strong, powerful man would draw from the well for all the drawers, sparing them the toil of drawing. The one who draws (al-mātiḥ) is called by a verb with a two-dot letter above.

God Most High mentioned Musa's (peace be upon him) drawing for the two daughters of Shu'ayb when he saw them held back from mingling in the herding. The Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in his dream his drawing on the well, then the drawing of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), then the drawing of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him).

Then it was borrowed, or made a metaphor, for taking turns and exchanging in passing cups of drink. al-A'sha said:

"I shared with them the twigs of basil, reclining, and wine, sharp, whose filter is moist."

The meaning: some of them pour wine for others and hand it to them, out of preference and honor.

It was also said: their tanāzuʿ of the cup is each one pulling another's cup toward himself for playfulness, as Imru' al-Qays said in playfulness over food:

Page 53

"So the virgins kept throwing at one another with its meat and fat, like the fringes of twisted silk."

The kās is a vessel from which wine is drunk, without a handle or spout, and it is feminine. It may be meant as the well-known vessel, or as the genus. His saying in Surat al-Saffat was mentioned: ﴿They are given to drink from a cup of flowing wine﴾ [al-Saffat: 45]. The intended meaning is not that they drink from one cup by each taking it from another.

It may also be that by "the cup" is meant the wine, which is an application of the name of the container to what it contains, like the saying "the valley flowed." As al-A'sha said: "I shared with them the twigs of basil" (the verse mentioned above).

The clause ﴿free of idle talk and sinful conduct﴾ may be a description of the cup, and the pronoun in ﴿free of idle talk therein﴾ refers to the cup, so that the cup is described as ﴿free of idle talk therein and sinful conduct﴾.

If the cup is understood as the well-known vessel, then the sense is: no idle talk and no sinful conduct for its owner; for "fī" here is the figurative sense of place, which is interpreted as accompaniment (mulābasa), as in His saying, ﴿and strive for God with the striving due to Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, "fa-fīhimā" (i.e., "to your parents"), so "strive" means: strive by being dutiful to them. Or "fī" is interpreted in the sense of causation, as in the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat she confined until it died of hunger."

If the cup is understood as meaning the wine, then "fī" is used figuratively for causation, i.e., no idle talk arising from its drinking. The meaning in both cases is that idle talk and sin, such as insults, beating and the like, do not mingle with its drinkers; that is, the wine for which the cup is used is not like the wines of this world.

The clause ﴿free of idle talk therein and sinful conduct﴾ may also be a resumptive independent sentence arising from the clause ﴿they pass around among themselves a cup﴾, with the pronoun in "therein" referring to the gardens in His saying ﴿Indeed, the righteous are in gardens﴾ [al-Tur: 17], like the pronoun in "therein, a cup." Then the clause carries the sense of a concluding summary (tadhyīl), since if idle talk and sinful conduct are negated from being in the Garden, they are negated from being in the cup of the people of Paradise's drinking.

Similar to these two aspects is His saying, ﴿Indeed, for the righteous is a place of triumph﴾ [al-Naba': 31], ﴿gardens and vineyards﴾ [al-Naba': 32], up to His saying ﴿They hear therein no idle talk or lying﴾ [al-Naba': 35] in Surat al-Naba'.

Al-laghw: useless speech and babbling that proceeds from a defect of reason.

Al-ta'thīm: whatever its doer is made sinful for, by the law or by custom, of deed or word, such as beating, insulting, tearing clothes, and what resembles the actions of madmen from the effects of revelry, which drinking companions generally do not avoid. The people of Paradise are exempt from all of that, because they belong to the world of realities and perfections, so they are wise and learned. The people of intellect from the Jahiliyya already prided themselves on being free of such things, and among them were those who guarded against the slips that arise and forbade wine to themselves, like Qays ibn 'Asim.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿lā laghwun fīhā wa lā ta'thīmun﴾ with both nouns in the nominative, taking "lā" as resembling "laysa." Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read them with fatḥa, taking "lā" as resembling "inna." These are two modes of negating an indefinite noun when the meaning of singularity is not admissible. Similar is her saying in the "Hadith of Umm Zar'": "My husband is like the night of Tihama: neither hot nor cold, neither fear nor weariness," where the four indefinites were narrated both with nominative and accusative.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 24:

It is conjoined to the clause ﴿They will pass around to one another a cup﴾ [al-Tur: 23], so it is part of its completion and stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), like it. It is expressed in the present tense to indicate renewal and recurrence, meaning: this does not cease, unlike the pleasures of this world, which must come to an end at limits where they stop, so that their people come to dislike further indulgence in them, such as intoxication (ghawl), exhaustion (ilṭibaq), and stomach ache from drinking wine, and like satiety from eating food, and everything else that produces inability to increase in pleasure and makes increase a pain.

Since the verb ﴿yaṭūfu﴾ ("goes around") indicates that the young boys serve them with what gives them pleasure, it also indicates the renewal of the serving and the renewal of the going around, and all of this has become a pleasure from which there is no weariness.

﴿Some of them turn to others, questioning one another.﴾ ﴿They say: "Indeed, we were before this, among our people, fearful [of Allah's punishment].﴾ ﴿So Allah bestowed His favour upon us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. This is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿They will pass around among themselves a cup﴾ [al-Tur: 23]. The implied construction is: "While some of them have turned to others, questioning one another," meaning that in those states they have turned to one another, questioning.

Since the joining of their offspring to them (ilḥāq dhurriyyātihim bihim) entails their sharing in the bliss, as was mentioned earlier at the words ﴿We will join their offspring to them﴾, this questioning takes place among all of them, both the forebears and the offspring, as questioners and as those questioned.

The pronoun in "some of them" (baʿḍuhum) refers to the God-fearing (al-muttaqūn) and to their offspring.

The clause "they say" (qālū) explains the clause "they question one another" (yatasāʾalūn), in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying: "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 120]. The pronoun in "they say" refers to both groups, meaning that each group among the questioners says this statement to the other group.

Ishfāq (fearfulness) is the anticipation of something disliked, and it is the opposite of hope. This anticipation varies among the questioners according to the variation in what necessitates it, namely shortcoming in fulfilling the obligations of the duty, or disobedience. For this reason, it is stronger on the side of the offspring of the believers, who were joined to their forebears without having earned it.

Perhaps it is more evident on the side of the offspring in the sense of gratitude, because their forebears are of their own family (ahl). They know that their offspring were fearful of the punishment of Allah, Exalted is He, or they are in the position of one who knows this from observing their conduct in fulfilling the obligations of the duty. Likewise, the forebears, in relation to those who know their condition from among their companions, or who hear from them their fearfulness and their seeking of forgiveness. The object of "fearful" (mushfiqīn) is omitted, because it is indicated by ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾.

On this reading, the meaning of "in" (fī) is locative (ẓarfiyya).

The phrase ﴿among our people﴾ (fī ahlinā) is connected to "we were" (kunnā), meaning: when we were among our folk in the world. Here "ahl" (family) carries the sense of "āl" (kin).

It is also permissible that the statement is issued by those who believed, addressing their offspring who were joined to them, and who had not supposed that they would be joined to them. The meaning would then be: "Indeed, we were before, fearful for your sake," so "in" (fī) is figurative locative (ẓarfiyya majāziyya), indicating causation, meaning: fearful on your account. Since the punishment of the offspring grieves their fathers, the protection of the offspring from it is treated as the protection of their fathers, so they say: ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾, in an exaggeration of gratitude on their part and on the part of their offspring, meaning: He bestowed His favour upon us all and protected us all from the punishment of the scorching wind.

"Al-Samūm" (with an open sīn) originally is the name of a wind that blows from an extremely hot direction, so it is dry and intensely hot. It is well known in the lands of the Arabs, and it destroys whoever inhales it. Here it is applied to the wind of Hell by way of approximation to a familiar matter, just as it was applied to the fiery element in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the samūm﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 27] in the chapter of al-Ḥijr. All of this is approximation to the familiar.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before﴾ is a justification for the favour of Allah upon them and a praise of Allah, that He responded to them. The meaning is: we used to call upon Him before this day, that is, in the world. The object of "call upon Him" (nadʿūhu) is omitted for generality, meaning: we used to supplicate to Him concerning our affairs. The cause of generality enters initially, and it is the supplication for themselves and for their offspring for salvation from the Fire and for attaining the bliss of Paradise.

Since this statement, in the reality of the matter, can only issue from inspiration and knowledge, it is evidence that the supplication of the righteous for their children and offspring is hoped to be answered, just as it indicates the answering of the supplication of righteous children for their parents. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three," and he mentioned among them "a righteous child who prays for him."

His saying, ﴿Indeed, He is the Most Good, the Most Merciful﴾, was recited by Nāfiʿ, al-Kisāʾī and Abū Jaʿfar with an open hamza in (annahu), reading it as the preposition (lām) being omitted in a regular manner with (anna), which here is the lām of causation, justifying "we call upon Him." The majority (al-Jumhūr) recited it with a kasra on the hamza of "inna," and the position of its clause is causation.

"Al-Barr" means the one who does good with gentleness.

"Al-Raḥīm" means the one of intense mercy, and it was discussed earlier in the commentary on Surat al-Fātiḥa.

The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) serves to convey restriction (ḥaṣr), and it restricts the two attributes of al-Barr and al-Raḥīm to Allah, Exalted is He. This is a restriction of claim (qaṣr iddiʿāʾī) for emphasis, since the goodness and mercy of others are not counted as significant in comparison with the goodness and mercy of Allah, in terms of strength, for others cannot reach in beneficence and mercy the level that belongs to Allah. It is also restricted in terms of the generality of its object, and in terms of permanence, since Allah is al-Barr in this world and the Hereafter, while others are good only at certain times in this world and possess nothing in the Hereafter.

The clause "they say" (qālū) explains the clause "they question one another" (yatasāʾalūn), in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying: "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 120]. The pronoun in "they say" refers to both groups, meaning that each group among the questioners says this statement to the other group.

Ishfāq (fearfulness) is the anticipation of something disliked, and it is the opposite of hope. This anticipation varies among the questioners according to the variation in what necessitates it, namely shortcoming in fulfilling the obligations of the duty, or disobedience. For this reason, it is stronger on the side of the offspring of the believers, who were joined to their forebears without having earned it.

Perhaps it is more evident on the side of the offspring in the sense of gratitude, because their forebears are of their own family (ahl). They know that their offspring were fearful of the punishment of Allah, Exalted is He, or they are in the position of one who knows this from observing their conduct in fulfilling the obligations of the duty. Likewise, the forebears, in relation to those who know their condition from among their companions, or who hear from them their fearfulness and their seeking of forgiveness. The object of "fearful" (mushfiqīn) is omitted, because it is indicated by ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾.

On this reading, the meaning of "in" (fī) is locative (ẓarfiyya).

The phrase ﴿among our people﴾ (fī ahlinā) is connected to "we were" (kunnā), meaning: when we were among our folk in the world. Here "ahl" (family) carries the sense of "āl" (kin).

It is also permissible that the statement is issued by those who believed, addressing their offspring who were joined to them, and who had not supposed that they would be joined to them. The meaning would then be: "Indeed, we were before, fearful for your sake," so "in" (fī) is figurative locative (ẓarfiyya majāziyya), indicating causation, meaning: fearful on your account. The meaning of ﴿So Allah bestowed His favour upon us﴾ is that He bestowed favour upon us by pardoning you, so He removed sorrow from us and protected us from His punishing you with the Fire. Since the punishment of the offspring grieves their fathers, the protection of the offspring from it is treated as the protection of their fathers, so they say: ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾, in an exaggeration of gratitude on their part and on the part of their offspring, meaning: He bestowed His favour upon us all and protected us all from the punishment of the scorching wind.

"Al-Samūm" (with an open sīn) originally is the name of a wind that blows from an extremely hot direction, so it is dry and intensely hot. It is well known in the lands of the Arabs, and it destroys whoever inhales it. Here it is applied to the wind of Hell by way of approximation to a familiar matter, just as it was applied to the fiery element in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of the samūm﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 27] in the chapter of al-Ḥijr. All of this is approximation to the familiar.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before﴾ is a justification for the favour of Allah upon them and a praise of Allah, that He responded to them. The meaning is: we used to call upon Him before this day, that is, in the world. The object of "call upon Him" (nadʿūhu) is omitted for generality, meaning: we used to supplicate to Him concerning our affairs. The cause of generality enters initially, and it is the supplication for themselves and for their offspring for salvation from the Fire and for attaining the bliss of Paradise.

Since this statement, in the reality of the matter, can only issue from inspiration and knowledge, it is evidence that the supplication of the righteous for their children and offspring is hoped to be answered, just as it indicates the answering of the supplication of righteous children for their parents. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three," and he mentioned among them "a righteous child who prays for him."

His saying, ﴿Indeed, He is the Most Good, the Most Merciful﴾, was recited by Nāfiʿ, al-Kisāʾī and Abū Jaʿfar with an open hamza in (annahu), reading it as the preposition (lām) being omitted in a regular manner with (anna), which here is the lām of causation, justifying "we call upon Him." The majority (al-Jumhūr) recited it with a kasra on the hamza of "inna," and the position of its clause is causation.

"Al-Barr" means the one who does good with gentleness.

"Al-Raḥīm" means the one of intense mercy, and it was discussed earlier in the commentary on Surat al-Fātiḥa.

The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) serves to convey restriction (ḥaṣr), and it restricts the two attributes of al-Barr and al-Raḥīm to Allah, Exalted is He. This is a restriction of claim (qaṣr iddiʿāʾī) for emphasis, since the goodness and mercy of others are not counted as significant in comparison with the goodness and mercy of Allah, in terms of strength, for others cannot reach in beneficence and mercy the level that belongs to Allah. It is also restricted in terms of the generality of its object, and in terms of permanence, since Allah is al-Barr in this world and the Hereafter, while others are good only at certain times in this world and possess nothing in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 29:

﴿So remind, for by the blessing of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer (kahin) nor a madman.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of everything that preceded it, from His saying ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾ [al-Tur: 7]. For it included consolation for the Messenger ﷺ regarding the denial of those who denied and their slander against him. This is followed by this verse because among the people there are those who believe in him and are certain that Allah sent him, together with what has been prepared for both groups. So what that contained required that in the continuation of reminding there is a wisdom which Allah intended, namely that some of the deniers would desist from their denial and that the believers would increase in deep immersion in their faith. Therefore it was made a consequence of that that Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to persist in reminding.

Thus the imperative is used to request continuity, like ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 136]. Since the effect of reminding is more important with regard to the group of deniers, so that whoever has his heart opened to faith may be guided, that which would increase the Prophet ﷺ in steadfastness in reminding was taken into account, namely clearing him of what they confront him with in their saying to him: "He is a soothsayer," or "He is a madman." So Allah steadied the heart of His Messenger ﷺ and informed him that his exoneration

صفحة ٥٩
from that is a blessing which his Lord bestowed upon him, the Exalted. Thus this statement was made a consequence of the command to remind, with His saying ﴿So you, by the blessing of your Lord, are neither a soothsayer nor a madman.﴾ The "bi" in ﴿bi-ni'mati rabbika﴾ indicates accompaniment (mulabasah), and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "anta" (you).

The negation of these two attributes from him, in addressing one like him who deserves to be described with the attributes of perfection, indicates that the purpose of the negation is another aim, which here is the refutation of the attribution of those who ascribed these to him, as in His saying ﴿And your companion is not a madman﴾ [al-Takwir: 22]. For this reason His subsequent saying ﴿Or do they say, "A poet"﴾ [al-Tur: 30], explicitly mentioning some of their statements, was a fitting follow-up. Thus it is known that what was negated of him in what precedes is a saying from among their sayings.

This noble expression includes features suited to glorifying the one it is addressed to: it was framed in a nominal sentence structure, so it is said "ma anta bi-kahin" (you are not a soothsayer) rather than "falasta bi-kahin" (you are not a soothsayer), to indicate the permanence of the content of this report.

The predicate-subject order was also altered, though the expected order would place the predicate first, namely "kahin" or "majnun", because the context calls for emphasis on the predicate. Yet emphasis on the pronoun (the subject) was more preferable here, due to what it contains of recalling his status, which signals that it is something great. It also conveyed that the intended meaning is that he is characterized by the report, not merely the act of reporting it, as in our saying: "The Messenger eats food and marries women." It also conveyed a restrictive (qasr idafi) sense by contextual indication, to reverse what they say or believe from their saying: "He is a soothsayer or a madman," following the manner of His saying ﴿And you are not, against us, mighty﴾ [Hud: 91].

The negated predicate was linked with the superfluous "bi" to affirm the negation, so two emphases occurred in the speech. The circumstantial clause was placed before the predicate, or the parenthetical clause between the subject and predicate, to hasten the joy and to show that Allah bestowed upon him exoneration from these two attributes.

Reference to the Divine Name was turned away from the proper noun (Allah) to defining it by the genitive construction and describing Him as the Lord (al-Rabb), to convey His gentle kindness toward His Messenger ﷺ, because He is his Lord, so He nurtures him and manages his benefit; and so that the genitive construction conveys the honouring of the one it is attributed to.

صفحة ٦٠
His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So you, by the blessing of your Lord, are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ is a reply to the saying of Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, who said of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "He is a soothsayer," and to 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt when he said, "He is a madman." That it is a reply to a saying that preceded is indicated by the fact that after it He followed with ﴿Or do they say, "A poet"﴾ [al-Tur: 30], and what will occur and what is hidden of what is yet to be.

The kahin (soothsayer) is one who claims knowledge of what will happen of affairs and what is hidden of what is yet to be, and reports it in speech with short rhymed phrases (asjac). The original word was established for this meaning and was not derived; its counterpart in Hebrew is (kohen), the guardian of the Law and its jurist, who is from the sons of (Levi). The mention of soothsaying was already made at His saying ﴿Nor have the devils brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 210] in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

In refuting his being a soothsayer or a madman, mere negation was sufficient without argument, because mere reflection on the state of the Prophet ﷺ is enough to establish the absence of those two attributes from him. Therefore, to refute his being characterized by them, nothing more is needed than the report of their negation, for its proof is observation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 30:

﴿Or do they say, "A poet, for whom we await the vicissitudes of fate"?﴾.

If the "am" (أم) is stripped of the function of conjunction, then the sentence is a fresh resumption (isti'naf bayani, explanatory resumption); otherwise it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the sentence ﴿So you, by the grace of your Lord, are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ [al-Tur: 29].

On the authority of al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi, the grammarian), every "am" in Surat al-Tur is interrogative and not a conjunction, meaning that the meaning rests on the interrogation and not on the conjunction of single words. This is a clear rule. Its intent is that the interrogative is implied after "am," and it is "am" in the sense of disconnection (munqati'a), serving to turn away (idrab) from their statement that was rejected by His words ﴿So you, by the grace of your Lord, are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ [al-Tur: 29], in order to transition to another statement, which is their saying: "He is a poet, for whom we await the vicissitudes of fate." The particle (بل) (bal, "rather") was avoided, though it is more well known for the transitional idrab, for the purpose that (أم) includes interrogation. The meaning is: "Rather, do they say he is a poet, etc.?" The established interrogation is one of denial (inkari).

The occasion of this transition from the command to the Prophet ﷺ to persist in admonition points to their statements by which they reject his call. When some of them were alluded to by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So you, by the grace of your Lord, are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ [al-Tur: 29], He moved on to refuting another attribute by which they triple the two attributes mentioned before it, namely the attribute of "poet."

al-Tabari narrated from Qatadah, who said: some of the people said: "Wait for Muhammad ﷺ to meet death; it will suffice you against him, as it sufficed you against the poet of the sons of so-and-so and the poet of the sons of so-and-so." They did not specify the name of the poet, nor that he used to satirize the disbelievers of Quraysh.

And from al-Dahhak and Mujahid: Quraysh gathered in the House of Assembly (dar al-Nadwa), and their opinions about Muhammad ﷺ multiplied. The Banu 'Abd al-Dar said: "He is a poet; wait for him for the vicissitudes of fate, for he will perish as Zuhayr, al-Nabigha and al-A'sha perished." They dispersed upon this statement, and this verse was revealed, relating their statement as they had said it. That is, there is no specific connection in the speech between the claim that he is a poet and awaiting death for him, because the vicissitudes of fate befall the poet, the soothsayer and the madman alike. The verb "yaqulun" came in the present tense to indicate the renewal of that saying from them. "Tarabbus" is an intensive form of "rabs," which means waiting.

Here "rayb" means the calamities (hadathan), and it has been explained as the changes of time (sarf al-dahr). From Ibn 'Abbas: "Rayb" in the Qur'an means doubt, except for one place in al-Tur: ﴿rayb al-manun﴾.

The "ba'" in "bihi" may be causal, meaning "because of him," i.e., "we await for his sake," so the "ba'" is connected to "natarabbasu." It may also be for accompaniment (mula'abah), connected to "rayb al-manun" as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from it, placed before its referent, meaning the descent of the vicissitudes of fate upon him.

"Al-Manun" is among the names of death and among the names of time, and it may be masculine. It has been explained by both meanings. When it is explained as death, the genitive construction of "rayb" to it is explanatory (bayaniyya), i.e., the calamity which is death. When "al-manun" is explained as time, the genitive construction retains its original sense, i.e., the calamities of time such as death, or departure from the land, or returning to his call; thus "rayb al-manun" is a genus. They mentioned in their statement the words "so he will perish," so it is possible that they meant to clarify the doubt of death, or that they meant it as an example of the doubt of time. Both possibilities apply to the verse, because it relates their statement.

صفحة ٦٢
"Rayb al-manun" has occurred in Arabic speech with both meanings. Of its occurrence in the sense of death is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

Do you grieve from death and its doubt, while time does not blame whoever laments?

And of its occurrence in the sense of the calamities of time is the verse of al-A'sha:

Did she see a man, al-A'sha, whom the doubt of death harmed, and a time of decay and senility?

He meant that the calamities of time harmed his person, and did not mean the striking of death as Abu Dhu'ayb meant.

Since the negation of his being a poet is an evident matter sufficiently established by mere reflection, the Qur'an did not undertake to argue for its refutation; rather, their statement included that they were awaiting that what befell the poets, who are among the people, should befall him.

So God, Exalted is He, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to answer them concerning this statement by saying: ﴿Wait, for I am with you among those who wait﴾ [al-Tur: 31]. This is a fair answer, for awaiting the befalling of the calamities of time upon either party, or the arrival of death, is a shared obligation; neither of us knows what will befall the other.

[Page 63]

The sentence ﴿قُلْ تَرَبَّصُوا﴾ (Say: "Wait"), is given without a conjunction (*fasl*, disjunction), because it occurs in the context of dialogue (*muhawara*). It follows the sentence ﴿يَقُولُونَ شاعِرٌ﴾ ("They say, 'He is a poet'") [al-Tur: 30], and so on. When someone is commanded to say something, it is as though he were told, "Say," and so he is commanded to say it. A similar example is His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ مَن يُعِيدُنا قُلِ الَّذِي فَطَرَكم أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ﴾ (They will say, "Who will restore us?" Say, "He who originated you the first time") [al-Isra: 51].

The imperative in ﴿تَرَبَّصُوا﴾ is used to express equalization (*taswiyah*), meaning: it is all the same to me, whether they wait for me or not. Following from this, He says ﴿فَإنِّي مَعَكم مِنَ المُتَرَبِّصِينَ﴾ (then indeed I am with you among those who wait), meaning: indeed I am waiting for you just as you are waiting for me, since neither of us knows which of us will be struck by the vicissitudes of fate first.

The emphasis of the statement by *inna* ("indeed") in His saying ﴿فَإنِّي مَعَكم مِنَ المُتَرَبِّصِينَ﴾ is to treat the addressees as if they were someone who denies that he waits for them as they wait for him. This is because, through their delusion, they limited themselves to saying that they wait for him in order to see his destruction. Thus this is an instance of treating a non-denier as a denier.

The *ma'iyyah* (being "with") in His saying ﴿مَعَكم﴾ apparently indicates sharing in the attribute of waiting.

Since His saying ﴿مِنَ المُتَرَبِّصِينَ﴾ implicitly carries the phrase "for you" (*bikum*) in response to their saying ﴿نَتَرَبَّصُ بِهِ رَيْبَ المَنُونِ﴾ (We wait for him to suffer the vicissitudes of fate) [al-Tur: 30], the statement contains an indication that he will remain with them, watching for their destruction when its signs appear. This alludes to the Battle of Badr, when death and capture befell them among the calamities of the time. Thus the verse alludes to the explicit statement of His saying in Surat al-Bara'ah: ﴿قُلْ هَلْ تَرَبَّصُونَ بِنا إلّا إحْدى الحُسْنَيَيْنِ ونَحْنُ نَتَرَبَّصُ بِكم أنْ يُصِيبَكُمُ اللَّهُ بِعَذابٍ مِن عِنْدِهِ أوْ بِأيْدِينا فَتَرَبَّصُوا إنّا مَعَكم مُتَرَبِّصُونَ﴾ (Say: "Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes? And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him or at our hands. So wait; indeed we are waiting with you") [al-Tawbah: 52]. He said here ﴿مِنَ المُتَرَبِّصِينَ﴾ only to indicate that the Prophet (ﷺ) waits for them, for the vicissitudes of fate, within the group of those who wait among the believers. This is what appears in the verse of Surat al-Bara'ah, spoken on the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers.

The composition of the speech in this verse has been arranged to suit the transition from one purpose to another. This is by means of what it was furnished with, namely a semblance of *tadhyil* (appended conclusion), in His saying ﴿قُلْ تَرَبَّصُوا فَإنِّي مَعَكم مِنَ المُتَرَبِّصِينَ﴾, since the verse-ending (*fasilah*) was completed by it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 32:

﴿Or do their minds command them to this?﴾.

This is a transition of change (idrab intiqal), prompted by the meaning of astonishment at their condition contained in the rhetorical denial question implied after "am" (or): how do they say such a statement as the previous one, and does this settle in their perception while they claim to be people of intellect, whose conditions of people are not confused for them? They do not fail to know that Muhammad ﷺ is not in the state of soothsayers, nor of madmen, nor of poets. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira refused to say such a thing about him in a well-known story.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Quraysh were called "people of minds (ahlam) and intellect (nuha)." The meaning is: do their supposed minds command them to this statement?

The reference in His words "this" is to the statement mentioned, which was alluded to in His words ﴿So you, by the blessing of your Lord, are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ [al-Tur: 29], and explicitly stated in His words ﴿Or do they say, "A poet; we await for him the misfortune of time"﴾ [al-Tur: 30]. This is like what one who blames a sensible person for an action says, which is not in his character to be ignorant of its corruption: "Are you sensible? Or does a sensible person do this of his own accord?" And of this kind is what Allah related about the people of Shu'ayb, when they said to him ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning﴾ [Hud: 87].

Al-hilm (forbearance/mind) means intellect. Al-Raghib said: it is what prevents the flaring of anger. In al-Qamus, it is patience (anah). In Ma'arij al-Nur: al-hilm is an innate faculty that causes its possessor to deal gently and softly with one who has wronged him or disturbed the balance of his nature.

The meaning of denying that their minds command them to this is that sound minds do not command the like of it, and there is in this an allusion that they have wasted their minds when they said that; for minds do not command the like of it, so they are like one who has no mind. This is the interpretation of what is reported, that the disbeliever has no intellect. They said: the disbeliever has only the mind (dhihn), and the mind accepts knowledge as a whole, whereas the intellect (aql) distinguishes knowledge and measures the measures for the limits of command and prohibition.

The command in "do they command them" is used metaphorically for impelling: that is, their minds impel them to this statement.

* * *

﴿Or are they a transgressing people?﴾.
This is also a transition of change (idrab intiqali), connected to what precedes it, moving to a question about their being characterized by transgression. The implied interrogation is used either for doubt, so that the doubt prompts reflection on their condition and one believes that they are transgressors, or it is used for affirmation to every listener, since he finds them transgressing.

The insertion of the word "people" (qawm) prepares for transgression being one of the constituents of the true nature of peoplehood among them, as we mentioned in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Surely there are signs for a people who understand﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surat al-Baqara; that is, transgression had become rooted in them and mixed into their souls, driving them to statements like those.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 33–34:

[Page 65]
﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ ﴿Rather, they do not believe.﴾ ﴿Then let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful.﴾

This is a continuation, linked to His saying ﴿Or do they say, "A poet"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30], etc. This is a report of their denial that the Qur'an is revelation from Allah. They claimed that the Prophet ﷺ had invented it and attributed it to Allah. So the interrogative is a rejection of their statement, and they had indeed greatly multiplied their slander against it and conspired together over it. For this reason, in reporting it about them, the form "yaqulun" (they say), which indicates renewal and repetition, was used.

And al-taqawwul (invention) is attributing a speech to someone who did not say it. It takes the speech itself as its direct object, and it takes the one to whom it is attributed with the preposition 'ala (upon). Allah the Exalted said ﴿And if he had invented against Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44] ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 45], the verse. The pronoun of object in taqawwalahu refers to the Qur'an, understood from the context.

The refutation began with His saying ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾ in order to hasten their rejection before presenting the proof against them, and so that the mention of the argument, which follows from their saying "they do not believe," would come as a second proof. The meaning of "they do not believe" is that the proofs of the Prophet's ﷺ freedom from inventing the Qur'an are clear to them, but those who make this claim refuse to believe. So they rush to slander without reflection and put forward excuses to conceal their obstinacy.

Since their statement was a slander against the Qur'an, which is the miracle establishing the truthfulness of Muhammad's ﷺ message, and since their claim that he invented it on Allah from his own self could be accepted by the common people, the Qur'an addressed the refutation of this by challenging them to produce something like this Qur'an, saying ﴿then let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful﴾, meaning: truthful in their claim that Muhammad ﷺ invented it from his own self. Thus their inability to produce something like it is evidence that they are liars.

The basis of the implication is that Muhammad ﷺ is one of the Arabs and speaks in their tongue. So equality between him and them in the capacity to compose speech is established. Had the Qur'an been said by Muhammad ﷺ, some of the eloquent elite of the Arabs would have been capable of composing its like. Since Allah challenged them to produce something like the Qur'an, while among them were their eloquent ones, their poets, and their orators, and they were all united in disbelief, their inability

[Page 66]
to produce something like the Qur'an indicates the inability of humans to produce the Qur'an. For this reason the Exalted said in Surah Hud ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ [Hud: 13] ﴿And if they do not respond to you, then know that it was revealed with the knowledge of Allah﴾ [Hud: 14].

As He the Exalted said ﴿Indeed, they do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33].

And iti'a (producing) a thing means bringing it from another place. This verb was chosen over the like of "then let them say something like it" for the purpose of leaving them no excuse, by being satisfied from them with bringing speech like it, even if from someone other than themselves. It has been mentioned, at His saying the Exalted in Surah al-Baqarah ﴿Then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], that it may carry two meanings: "Then produce a surah of the likeness of the Qur'an," or "Then produce from the likeness of the Messenger ﷺ," meaning from any one of mankind.

And al-hadith (the statement/narrative): reporting of events. The original sense of hawadith is recent occurrences, then it was extended to be applied to occurrences even if they are old, as in their saying "the events of such a year." This was followed by the application of hadith to report in general, and it was further extended to be applied to speech even if it is not a report. Among this is the application of hadith to the speech of the Prophet ﷺ.

So it is possible that hadith here is applied to speech metaphorically by the relation of generality, meaning: "then let them produce speech like it," i.e., on one of the subjects that the Qur'an contains, not specifically reports. And it is possible that hadith here is applied to reports, meaning: "then let them produce reports like the stories of the Qur'an." This would be a lowering of the challenge for them, since speaking in reports is easier for the speaker than originating the subjects on which he speaks. For they used to say that the Qur'an is ﴿tales of the ancients﴾ [al-An'am: 25], i.e., reports about past nations. So it was said to them: "Then let them produce reports like its reports," because producing the like of what is in the Qur'an of knowledge, legislation, and proofs is beyond the capacity of their minds, and the most they can do is understand it when they hear it.

The meaning of likeness in His saying "mithlihi" (its like) is likeness in its eloquence and rhetoric. These are qualities they perceive when they hear them, but their faculties cannot encompass placing them in their own speech. We have explained the principles of the inimitability (i'jaz) in the tenth introduction of this commentary.

The imperative particle in "fal-ya'tu" (then let them produce) is used for the imperative of challenge, like His saying, relating the statement of Ibrahim: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258].

And His saying ﴿if they are truthful﴾ means: in their claim that he invented it. That is, if they do not produce speech like it, then they are liars. This is an urging on of their resolve to produce speech like the Qur'an, so that their failure to produce its like would be a proof of their lying. The arrangement of the speech in His saying ﴿then let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful﴾, placed in a position resembling a concluding phrase ending with the closing word (fasila), indicates that it is the end of one theme and that what follows begins another theme, as was previously mentioned in the arrangement of His saying ﴿Say, "Wait, for I am with you among those who wait."﴾ [al-Tur: 31].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 33–34:

[Page 65]
﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ ﴿Rather, they do not believe.﴾ ﴿Then let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful.﴾

This is a continuation, linked to His saying ﴿Or do they say, "A poet"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30], etc. This is a report of their denial that the Qur'an is revelation from Allah. They claimed that the Prophet ﷺ had invented it and attributed it to Allah. So the interrogative is a rejection of their statement, and they had indeed greatly multiplied their slander against it and conspired together over it. For this reason, in reporting it about them, the form "yaqulun" (they say), which indicates renewal and repetition, was used.

And al-taqawwul (invention) is attributing a speech to someone who did not say it. It takes the speech itself as its direct object, and it takes the one to whom it is attributed with the preposition 'ala (upon). Allah the Exalted said ﴿And if he had invented against Us some sayings﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44] ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [al-Haqqah: 45], the verse. The pronoun of object in taqawwalahu refers to the Qur'an, understood from the context.

The refutation began with His saying ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾ in order to hasten their rejection before presenting the proof against them, and so that the mention of the argument, which follows from their saying "they do not believe," would come as a second proof. The meaning of "they do not believe" is that the proofs of the Prophet's ﷺ freedom from inventing the Qur'an are clear to them, but those who make this claim refuse to believe. So they rush to slander without reflection and put forward excuses to conceal their obstinacy.

Since their statement was a slander against the Qur'an, which is the miracle establishing the truthfulness of Muhammad's ﷺ message, and since their claim that he invented it on Allah from his own self could be accepted by the common people, the Qur'an addressed the refutation of this by challenging them to produce something like this Qur'an, saying ﴿then let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful﴾, meaning: truthful in their claim that Muhammad ﷺ invented it from his own self. Thus their inability to produce something like it is evidence that they are liars.

The basis of the implication is that Muhammad ﷺ is one of the Arabs and speaks in their tongue. So equality between him and them in the capacity to compose speech is established. Had the Qur'an been said by Muhammad ﷺ, some of the eloquent elite of the Arabs would have been capable of composing its like. Since Allah challenged them to produce something like the Qur'an, while among them were their eloquent ones, their poets, and their orators, and they were all united in disbelief, their inability

[Page 66]
to produce something like the Qur'an indicates the inability of humans to produce the Qur'an. For this reason the Exalted said in Surah Hud ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ [Hud: 13] ﴿And if they do not respond to you, then know that it was revealed with the knowledge of Allah﴾ [Hud: 14].

As He the Exalted said ﴿Indeed, they do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33].

And iti'a (producing) a thing means bringing it from another place. This verb was chosen over the like of "then let them say something like it" for the purpose of leaving them no excuse, by being satisfied from them with bringing speech like it, even if from someone other than themselves. It has been mentioned, at His saying the Exalted in Surah al-Baqarah ﴿Then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], that it may carry two meanings: "Then produce a surah of the likeness of the Qur'an," or "Then produce from the likeness of the Messenger ﷺ," meaning from any one of mankind.

And al-hadith (the statement/narrative): reporting of events. The original sense of hawadith is recent occurrences, then it was extended to be applied to occurrences even if they are old, as in their saying "the events of such a year." This was followed by the application of hadith to report in general, and it was further extended to be applied to speech even if it is not a report. Among this is the application of hadith to the speech of the Prophet ﷺ.

So it is possible that hadith here is applied to speech metaphorically by the relation of generality, meaning: "then let them produce speech like it," i.e., on one of the subjects that the Qur'an contains, not specifically reports. And it is possible that hadith here is applied to reports, meaning: "then let them produce reports like the stories of the Qur'an." This would be a lowering of the challenge for them, since speaking in reports is easier for the speaker than originating the subjects on which he speaks. For they used to say that the Qur'an is ﴿tales of the ancients﴾ [al-An'am: 25], i.e., reports about past nations. So it was said to them: "Then let them produce reports like its reports," because producing the like of what is in the Qur'an of knowledge, legislation, and proofs is beyond the capacity of their minds, and the most they can do is understand it when they hear it.
