Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 35:

﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾

This is a transitional *idrab* (a shift from one topic to another, marked by "bal" or "am") to refute another form of their doubt about resurrection (*ba'th*). You have already learned at the beginning of the surah that one of its purposes is to establish resurrection and recompense. What follows it, the description of the Day of Recompense and the condition of its people, was required by connections (*munasabat*) that arose from those details. Once what those connections required had been fully addressed, the discourse turned back to proving the possibility of resurrection and refuting their doubt, which they justified by saying, for example, ﴿When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we truly be raised in a new creation?﴾ [al-Isra: 49].

So the words ﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾ and what follows are evidences that what God created at the beginning of creation is greater than the re-creation of man. This connects to His earlier words, ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾ [al-Tur: 7], because the doubt that was intended to be refuted by that statement is their saying, ﴿When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we truly be raised?﴾ [al-Isra: 49], and similar things.

The particle *min* (from) in ﴿from nothing﴾ may be for the beginning of origin (*li'l-ibtida'*). In that case the implied interrogative after *am* is affirmative in the sense of confirmation (*taqriri*). The meaning is: Do they admit that they were created after having been non-existent? Since they were created from non-existence in their first origination, they will be brought forth from non-existence in the second origination. This establishes the possibility of resurrection, and it has the same sense as His words, ﴿So let man consider from what he was created. He was created from a gushing fluid, emerging from between the backbone and the ribs. Indeed, He is able to return him [to life]﴾ [al-Tariq: 5–8], and His words, ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 104], and similar verses.

The meaning of *shay'* (thing) in this sense is "that which exists," so *ghayr shay'* (no thing) means "that which does not exist." The meaning is: Were they created from non-existence?

The *min* may also be causal (*li'l-ta'lil*). In that case the implied interrogative after *am* is a denial (*inkari*), and the noun *shay'* applies to whatever is suitable for the causal meaning derived from the causal particle *min*. The meaning is a denial that He created them without wisdom. This affirms that resurrection occurs for the sake of recompense for deeds, since recompense is required by the wisdom which the act of the Wisest of the wise never lacks. This has the same sense as His words, ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115], and His words, ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth. And indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ [al-Hijr: 85].

The particle *min* in this statement has a wondrous effect, since, by bearing both of its meanings, it is evidence for the possibility of resurrection, for its occurrence, and for the necessity of its occurrence, a necessity required by the supreme divine wisdom. Perhaps the departure from phrasing the statement in the form that is common in the affirmative interrogative (*istifham taqriri*), namely the negative form, as in "Were they not created from nothing?", and the departure from specifying what the word *ghayr* (other than/no) is attached to, in favor of an ambiguous word, *shay'* (thing), which was chosen for its suitability to bear both meanings, is from the highest level of eloquence.

Since the supposition that they were created from nothing is clearly false, it did not need an argument to refute it. Then He says:

* * *

﴿Or were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ ﴿Or did they create the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Tur: 35–36].

This is also a transitional *idrab*, and the implied interrogative after *am* is a denial. That is, "They are not the creators." Since they did not claim this, the denial is based on treating them as if they claimed to be creators.

The sentence is phrased in the form of restriction (*hasr*), whose method is the definition of both parts (*ta'rif al-juz'ayn*), as a restriction by specification (*qasr idafi*), to refute them by treating them as those who claim that they are the creators and not God. This is because they regarded as impossible what was beyond their power, and so they made it beyond the power of God. The meaning is: "Or are they the creators, not We?" That is, "We are the creators, not they."

The object of *al-khaliqun* (the creators) is omitted for the sake of generality, meaning "the creators of created things." On this interpretation al-Tabari proceeded, and the exegetes other than al-Tabari have supposed it to mean: "Or are they the creators of themselves?" It is as if they took the pronoun in ﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾ as evidence that the omitted element is the referent of that pronoun. There is no dispute about the impossibility of their being creators, so no attempt was made to argue for this negation.

The sentence ﴿Or did they create the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Tur: 36] appears to me to be a *badal* (substitute/apposition) of the sentence ﴿Or are they the creators?﴾. It is a detailed *badal* (*badal mufassal*) of a general statement (*mujmal*), if the omitted object of "the creators" is intended to be general and the heavens and the earth are meant in their own selves together with what is in them. Alternatively, it is a *badal ba'd min kull* (partial substitute for the whole), where the intended meaning is the very essence of the heavens and the earth. In that case the specific mention of the heavens and the earth is for the greatness of their creation.

The particle *am* is repeated for emphasis, just as the governing element of the substituted noun is repeated in the *badal*. The meaning is: "Or are they the creators of the heavens and the earth?"

The interrogative is a denial, and the statement is a *kinaya* (allusion/indirect expression) for the affirmation that God is the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

The meaning is that He who created the heavens and the earth is not incapable of re-creating bodies after death and annihilation. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them?﴾ [al-Isra: 99], that is, able to create the like of their bodies after they have ceased to exist.

Abrogation-free rendering follows: this is a refutation (idrab ibtal) of the content of the two preceding clauses, meaning: they were not created from nothing, nor did they create the heavens and the earth, for that is clear to them. So their denial of resurrection (al-ba'th) arises only from their not being certain in the places where certainty is to be found, namely the proofs that indicate the possibility of resurrection and that it is no more strange than the bringing into existence of the great creatures. Their denial of it is therefore only out of obstinate arrogance and determination upon disbelief.

The meaning: the matter is neither this nor that, but they do not have certainty about the resurrection, so they deny it without any proof or doubt; rather, obstinacy has taken hold of their hearts.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 37:

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾ This is a shift back to refuting their denial of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason the mode of address changed from report to addressing the Prophet (ﷺ). The principle on which their denial was founded was their assumption that, if God were to send a messenger from among humankind, the one more deserving of the message would be a great man from among the great men of their people, as God related of them: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8]. He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 31], meaning the city of Makkah and the city of al-Ta'if.

The meaning is: a refutation that they have any disposal over matters of lordship, such that they could make affairs follow their will, like the owner in his property and the manager in what he has been entrusted with. The interrogation is therefore one of denial, placing them, in their refutation of prophethood, in the position of one who has the treasuries of God, from which they bestow gifts on whom they wish and withhold from whom they wish, while they reject those they do not approve of.

Al-khaza'in (the treasuries): the plural of khazina (treasury), which is a chamber, or the chest in which provisions are stored, or wealth and whatever is precious with its keeper. This was discussed under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Set me over the treasuries of the land"﴾ [Yusuf: 55]. Here it is used metaphorically for what lies in God's knowledge and will of bestowing the bounty of others upon creatures, among which is the choosing of whomever He has prepared from among people to convey His message to humankind. It was previously mentioned in Surah al-An'am His saying: ﴿Say, "I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of God"﴾ [Al-An'am: 50]. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when a sign comes to them, they say, "We will not believe until we are given what was given to the messengers of God." God knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am: 124]. And He said: ﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses. They have no choice. Glory be to God, and exalted is He above what they associate﴾ [Al-Qasas: 68].

Here the method of brevity has been followed in argument, by referring them to a general matter that His saying ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾ has specified; because the situation is one of anger against them, for their audacity toward the Messenger (ﷺ) in negating the message from him with insolence, in their saying: "a soothsayer," "a madman," "a poet," etc. This differs from the verse of al-An'am, for that verse answered their presenting themselves as deserving to receive the message from God.

So His saying here, ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾, is like His saying in Surah Sad: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us? Nay, they are in doubt about My reminder. Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad: 8], and ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Almighty, the Bestower?﴾ [Sad: 9], and His saying in Surah al-Zukhruf: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 32].

The word 'inda is often used in the sense of ownership and exclusivity, as in His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ [Al-An'am: 59]. So the meaning is: Do they own the treasuries of your Lord, i.e., the treasuries which your Lord owns, as the idafa of treasuries to your Lord implies, in the manner of ﴿Has he knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ [Al-Najm: 35]. This has been expressed with the literal wording in His saying: ﴿Say, "If you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, then you would withhold them for fear of expenditure"﴾ [Al-Isra: 100].

* * *

"﴿Or are they the controllers?﴾"

This is a denial that they should have any disposal over the giving of God, exalted is He, even if less than the disposal of an owner, like the disposal of a trustee or treasurer; this is what is expressed by al-musaytirun (the controllers).

Al-musaytir: it is pronounced with ṣād or sīn at its beginning. It is the active participle of sayṭara (with ṣād or sīn), meaning to guard and to dominate. It is a verb derived from sayṭara, meaning to cut, and from it comes al-sātūr, which is an iron with which meat and bone are cut. The pattern fa'īl was formed from it for assimilation to the quadriliteral, as in their saying: baygara, meaning perished or was present, and baytara, meaning split, and haymana; and there is no fifth of these among verbs. Replacing the sīn with ṣād is a dialectal variant in it, like al-ṣirāṭ and al-sirāṭ.

The majority read al-muṣayṭirūn with ṣād. Qunbul from Ibn Kathir, Hisham from Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs in his transmission read it with sīn at its beginning.

In the meaning of the verse is His saying: ﴿Or do they apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [Al-Zukhruf: 32]. There is no evidence in the verse for this negation in His saying "Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord, or are they the controllers?", because its clarity is like fire on a mountain. The hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im has been mentioned earlier at the beginning of the tafsir of this surah, when he heard this verse and it was the cause of his conversion to Islam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 38:

﴿Or do they have a ladder by which they listen? Then let their listener bring a clear authority.﴾

When He negated that they had any strong or weak power over God's bounties to His servants, He followed it with the negation that they had any knowledge of what God has decreed for His servants, a knowledge that would entitle them to deny that God sends a human messenger or reveals to him. This is to refute their saying, "He has fabricated it" (taqawwalahu). Similar is their saying, ﴿We await for him the calamities of fate﴾ (al-Tur: 30), which implies that they are confident they will witness his destruction. The object of yastami'un (they listen) is omitted so that it covers any speech whose nature is to be heard: reports of unseen matters, whether about the future or about other things, whether actual or not.

In negating their knowledge of the unseen, He took the path of mockery toward them, by denying that they have a ladder (sullam) by which they climb to the sky in order to listen to what happens in the upper world, such as a matter that the angels or the people of the exalted assembly (ahl al-mala' al-a'la) receive and discuss among themselves, so that they might steal some of the knowledge that is hidden from people. It is known that there is no ladder connecting the people of the earth to the sky, and they know this, and everyone knows it.

From the name sullam it is known that it is an instrument for ascent, and from the mention of the heavens in the preceding verse it is known that what is meant is a ladder by which they ascend to the sky. Therefore it is described by ﴿by which they listen﴾, meaning: they ascend by it to the sky and listen while they are in it, that is, in its rungs, to the speech that takes place in the sky. The word fihi (in it) is an adverbial phrase of place (zarf mustaqirr) functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in yastami'un, meaning: they are situated in it, not leaving it, since it is not supposed that they descend from it to the courtyards of the sky.

The attribution of the listening to the pronoun of their group, on the understanding that the listener is their envoy on their behalf, follows the usual practice of Arabic speech of attributing the action of some of a tribe to all of it, when nothing prevents it from being their action, as in the saying: "The Banu Asad killed a stone." Do you not see that He said after this:

Page 73

﴿then let their listener come﴾, meaning: whoever among them listens on their behalf, that is, they sent him to listen. Such attribution is common in the Qur'an, and it was discussed under His saying ﴿And when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst torment﴾ (al-Baqarah: 49) and the verses following it in surah al-Baqarah.

"Fi" (in) indicates location, and it is a figurative location that has become so well known that it is equal to the literal sense. This is because the one who climbs a ladder is entirely upon it, so the ladder is to him as a container is to what it contains. Although in reality it indicates elevation (isti'la'), it spread in speech so that they say "sa'ida fi al-sullam" (he climbed in the ladder) and do not say "sa'ida 'ala al-sullam" (he climbed upon the ladder). Therefore it is considered a real locative sense, that is, a conventional real sense, unlike the locative in His saying ﴿And I will surely crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ (Ta-Ha: 71), because it is not known that one says "salabahu fi jidh'" (he crucified him in a trunk); rather one says "salabahu 'ala jidh'" (he crucified him upon a trunk). Therefore that usage is a metaphor. So there is no contradiction between the view of whoever claims that the locative sense is figurative and the view of whoever claims it is literal.

The fa' in ﴿then let their listener bring a clear authority﴾ introduces this challenging command as a consequence of the negation derived from the interrogative of denial. The meaning is: no listener among them brings evidence that shows the truth of their claim. The imperative lam here is used to express incapacitation (ta'jiz), as indicated by the absence of the very act of listening, by way of the interrogative of denial.

As-sultan means proof (hujjah), that is, a proof of their truthfulness in denying the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), or in claiming that he is on the brink of destruction.

What is meant by sultan is whatever indicates their knowledge of the unseen through signs, such as their saying: "The sign of our truthfulness in what we claim and what we heard from the speech of the exalted assembly is that it will happen tomorrow that such-and-such event occurs," for example, something that people have no means of knowing. Then it happens as they said, and their truthfulness in the rest of what they say is thereby inferred. This is the meaning of describing the sultan as mubin (clear), that is, the one that manifests the validity of the claim.

This is a challenge to them regarding their lying, and therefore it suffices that some of them bring a proof, rather than requiring all of them to do so, in the manner of His saying ﴿then bring a surah like it﴾ (Yunus: 38). That is: let whoever among them undertakes the listening bring a proof. This serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil) of the discourse, in the manner of what preceded in His saying ﴿Say: Wait, for I am with you among those who wait﴾ (al-Tur: 31) and His saying ﴿then let them bring a statement like it, if they are truthful﴾ (al-Tur: 34).

[Page 74]

﴿Or has He daughters while you have sons?﴾

When the denial that they have any access to the unseen from the Higher Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) had been established, refuting their claims concerning the matters of lordship (al-rububiyyah), it was followed by the refutation of their attribution of daughters to Allah, thoroughly refuting their illusions about the unseen matters of the higher world. Thus this sentence is parenthetical, placed between the sentence ﴿Or do they have a ladder?﴾ [al-Tur: 38] and the sentence ﴿Or do you ask them for a reward?﴾ [al-Tur: 40]. The interrogative is understood as a denial that Allah should have daughters.

The proof of the denial of the matter itself is the impossibility of offspring for Allah, the Exalted. However, since the minds of most of those addressed by this rebuttal were not prepared to grasp the proof of impossibility, and since their belief that Allah has daughters was objectionable, the rebuttal turned to a proof of refutation, and in refuting it, a persuasive (iqna'i) proof was employed by which they would perceive the absurdity of their opinion, namely His saying ﴿and you have sons﴾.

The sentence ﴿and you have sons﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun of the absent party. That is: how can Allah have daughters when you have sons, while you know that the male sex is more noble than the female sex in general, as indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ [al-Najm: 21] ﴿That, then, is an unfair division!﴾ [al-Najm: 22].

This is an exaggeration in censuring their statement. The intent is not that if they had attributed sons to Allah, their statement would have been acceptable, for they did not say that; therefore there is no point in refuting it.

The change from the third-person style, which had been followed from His saying ﴿Or do they say, "A poet"?﴾ [al-Tur: 30], to the second-person style is an iltifat (shift) of confrontation with them in the rebuttal, by means of the circumstantial sentence.

The placement of ﴿lakum﴾ (for you) before ﴿al-banun﴾ (the sons) serves to express exclusivity: that is, "for you are the sons, not Him"; thus they have sons and daughters, yet they claimed that Allah has nothing but daughters.

As for the placement of the prepositional phrase before the subject in ﴿Or has He daughters﴾, it is for the sake of emphasis on the Name of Majesty (Allah). The speech is concluded with the fasilah (verse-ending), because this is an independent purpose.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 40:

[Page 75]
﴿Or do you ask them for a reward, so that they are burdened with debt?﴾.
This is connected to His saying ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [al-Tur: 33] and His saying ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾ [al-Tur: 37], since all of that is a refutation of the causes that lead them to the claim that prophethood is negated from Muhammad (ﷺ). So, after he refuted the means of acquiring knowledge by which they claimed (it), he returned to refuting the motives that lead them to turn away from the call of the Messenger (ﷺ). For this reason, this statement came in the style of the speech to which it is joined, which is the style of addressing the Messenger (ﷺ). So here He said ﴿Or do you ask them for a reward﴾, and there He said ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾ [al-Tur: 37].

The interrogative implied after "am" (aw/am) is used for mockery of them, by treating them as one who fears lest the Messenger (ﷺ) ask them a reward for guiding them.

Mockery (al-tahakkum) is a metaphor founded on comparison, and the intended meaning of what is in the mockery is that what gave rise to the mockery is a matter that should not occur to the mind.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 41:**

﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write (it down)?﴾ This is the parallel of the transitional (al-idrab, a shift from one matter to another) and interrogative (al-istifham, a question) construction in His words ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of your Lord?﴾ [al-Tur: 37]. That is: "Rather, do they have the unseen, so that they write down what they find in it and relate it to the people?" That is, they do not possess the unseen so as to write it down. After He refuted their denial of Islam by stating that they are like those whom the Prophet ﷺ asked for a reward for conveying it, He followed this with another refutation: that they are like those who have looked into what is with God and found it contrary to what the Messenger ﷺ claimed to convey from God. So they write down what they have seen, and find it contradicting what the Messenger ﷺ brought.

Qatadah said: When they said ﴿We await for him the misfortunes of time﴾ [al-Tur: 30], God, exalted is He, said ﴿Or do they have the unseen?﴾, meaning: until they know when Muhammad will die, or what his affair will come to. Here, "al-ghayb" (the unseen) is a verbal noun used in the sense of a active participle, meaning: that which is hidden from the knowledge of people.

The definite article in "al-ghayb" is the definite article of the genus (al-jins, the class as a whole). The word "ʿindahum" (with them) indicates the meaning of exclusivity and monopoly, that is, they have monopolized the knowledge of the unseen and thus know what no one else knows.

The writing in His words ﴿so they write﴾ may be metaphorical (isti'arah) for a certain decision that admits no change, as in His words ﴿Your Lord has prescribed upon Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 54]. This is because the nature of a matter that one wishes to establish and to keep constant is that it be written and recorded, as al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"And do the desires undo what is in the scrolls?"

[Page 77]

In that case, the statement in His words ﴿so they write﴾ is used with its meaning of asserting a predicative relation.

In that case the statement in His words ﴿so they write﴾ is used in the sense of supposition, following the supposition of His words ﴿they have the unseen﴾, and it falls under the same category as His words ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 35], and His words ﴿He said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"﴾ [Maryam: 77], ﴿Has he looked into the unseen?﴾ [Maryam: 78].

The sum of the meaning is that they have no basis either for denying what they have rejected or for affirming what they have affirmed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 52, verse 42:

﴿Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve are the ones who will be plotted against.﴾

This is a transition from refuting their statements and nullifying their claims to nullifying their intentions and resolves to launch a night attack (tabyit) against the Messenger (ﷺ), against the believers, and against the call of Islam, with harm and failure. In this there is an exposure of their inner secrets and a warning to the believers to be wary of their scheming.

The object of "kaydan" (a plot) has been omitted so that it generalizes to everything they are able to plot. Thus this sentence serves as a completion (tatmim) that undoes their spinning of falsehoods, and as a concluding summary (tadhyil) encompassing every resolve that runs through the matters about which their statements were made.

Kayd (scheming) and makr (deception) are close in meaning, and both are the display of concealing harm, by way of concealment, to deceive the one intended to be harmed.

He shifted from the pronoun (idmar) to the noun (izhar) in His words ﴿fa-alladhina kafaru hum al-makidun﴾. The expected form by the rule would have been "fa-hum al-makidun," but the relative clause indicates the reason the scheming falls upon them: they disbelieved in Allah, so Allah defends His Messenger (ﷺ), the believers, and His religion against their scheming, and brings upon them what they intended to bring upon others.

The separating pronoun (damir al-fasl, a pronoun that separates subject and predicate) conveys restriction (qasr), meaning: it is those who disbelieved who are the ones plotted against, not those who intended the plot.

Page 78

The application of the term "kayd" to what Allah repays them with for their scheming, namely the undoing of their spinning of falsehoods, is an application by way of mushakalah (a figure in which a term is used for something else because of their correspondence in context), likening Allah's prolonging of favor to them until punishment befalls them, to the action of one who schemes against another. This is a clear threat to them. His words ﴿wa-yamkuruna wa-yamkuru Allah wa-Allahu khayru al-makirin﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] have already preceded in surah al-Anfal.

Among the manifestations of this threat is what befell them on the Day of Badr, when they did not expect it.

This is the last arrow in the quiver of refutation against them, and the most forceful shot at the figure of their disbelief, which is the figure of association (shirk), the most comprehensive of errors under which all other errors gather: their associating other deities alongside Allah.

Since what was censured of them from the beginning of the surah contradicted their statements and their intentions, and since what they were engaged in of shirk was greater, the enumeration of that against them was not left out, after its notoriety, once the purpose for which the discourse was driven had been fulfilled by this occasion. For this reason, this transition to it stands in the position of a concluding summation (tadhyil) for what precedes it, because it is an ascent to what is most important within its category, and the most important resembles the most general, so it served as a tadhyil. Its parallel in ascending to perfection within the category is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Freeing a slave, or feeding﴾ [al-Balad: 13] up to His words ﴿then he became of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17], the verse.

The words ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate﴾ have come as the completion of the tadhyil and the ending of the intended aim of exposing their condition.

It is clear that the interrogative implied after "am" (or) is a denunciatory interrogation (istifham inkari). The meaning is: if they see a fragment of the sky of what they asked to be a sign of your truthfulness, they will not submit, nor believe, nor abandon slander, but they will say, "This is a cloud." This meaning is narrated from Qatadah.

This is of the same kind as His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And if We opened for them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it,﴾ [al-Hijr: 14] ﴿they would surely say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people affected by magic."﴾ [al-Hijr: 15].

"Al-kisf" with a kasra on the fa' means a piece, and it is said: kasafahu. It has already been discussed in Surat al-Isra'.

And ﴿min al-sama'﴾ is an attribute of "kisfan," and "min" is partitive, meaning a piece of the parts of the sky, like the pieces that fall from shooting stars.

"Al-markum" means that which is piled up, one part above another; it is said: rakamahu rakman. It is the rain-bearing cloud. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Then He makes it layered (rukaman)﴾ [al-Nur: 43].

Page 80
The meaning: if that should happen in the future, they will say, "Cloud." This does not imply that it occurs, because the conditional particle only requires that the occurrence of its answer be contingent upon the occurrence of its protasis, were it to occur. "Sahabun markum" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and its estimate is: "It is a cloud," or "This is a cloud."
The intended meaning is that they say this out of obstinacy while being certain that it is not a cloud.

Since the intended meaning is that obstinacy is their nature, it is made a consequence that Allah's command to His Messenger ﷺ was to leave them, that is, to leave off presenting the signs to them, meaning: he should not ask Allah to manifest what they proposed of signs, because they do not propose these seeking proof, but they are obstinate. The intended meaning is not to leave off calling them and presenting the Qur'an to them.

The limit (ghayah) indicates that He leaves them forever, because after they are struck senseless, their argument will no longer be renewed with proofs and signs.

Al-Jumhur read "yulaqu" (they meet). Abu Ja'far read (yalqaw) without an alif after the lam.

The day in which they are struck senseless is the Day of Resurrection, at which whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on earth will be struck senseless.

The attribution of the day to their pronoun is because they became known for denying it and were recognized as "those who do not believe in the Hereafter." This is similar to the attribution (nisba) in the saying of the people of the principles of religion: "So-and-so is a Qadari," meaning that he does not believe in qadar. The meaning, by attributing him to qadar, is that he engages in discussing it; or because it is the day that was promised to them, so the attribution is for the slightest connection.

Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the angels will receive them, "This is your Day which you were promised."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103].

"Al-sa'q" is fainting from fear or terror. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. Its root is derived from "al-sa'iqah" (the thunderbolt), because the one struck by it faints or dies. It is said: sa'iqa, with fatha then kasra, and su'iqa with damma then kasra.
Al-Jumhur read "yas'aqun" with a fatha on the ya' (the third person masculine plural form), and Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read it with a damma on the ya'.

"Al-ighna'" means making another person rich, that is, not in need of what is required to meet his needs. When it is said: aghna 'anhu, its meaning is that he took his place in removing a need which it was his duty to fulfill, and it is used loosely by omitting its object, since it is evident from the context.

The intended meaning here is: it will not avail them anything of the punishment understood from the attribution of the day to their pronoun, and from the relative clause in His saying "in which they are struck senseless."

"Kaydu-hum" is an attribution of the verbal noun to its agent, meaning: what they plot with, which is what is indicated by His saying ﴿Or do they intend a plot?﴾ [al-Tur: 42], that is, they will not be able to plot on that Day as they used to in the world.

The meaning: they will have no plot by which it would avail them, in the manner of the saying of Imru' al-Qays: "On a faint track whose landmark is not guided by," that is, it has no landmark by which one is guided.

This negates for them any escape through means of their own doing. And it is conjoined to it

That is: indeed, for them there is a punishment in this world before the punishment of the Hereafter, and it is the punishment of hunger during the years of drought, and the punishment of the sword on the Day of Badr.

What is meant by ﴿the judgment of your Lord﴾ is what He has decreed and determined concerning the non-response of some of them and the delayed response of most of them.

The *lam* in His words ﴿for the judgment of your Lord﴾ may carry the sense of *'ala* ("upon"), so that it serves to govern the verb *isbir* ("be patient"), as in the Exalted's words ﴿and be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10].

And to warn them of an event that will befall them soon.

And it mentions the recompense of those who turn away and of those who are guided, and warns them against speaking about these matters by conjecture without evidence.

And to refute their analogy of the unseen world to the visible world, and that this is an error of opinion, while guidance from God has come to them contrary to it. An example of this is mentioned from the story of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, or the story of Ibn Abi Sarh.

And to establish resurrection and recompense.

**[p. 89]**

And to remind them of what befell the nations that associated partners with God before them, and of those messengers who came before Muhammad ﷺ, the bearers of religious laws.

And to warn them of an event that will befall them soon.

And of what intervenes in all this of parenthetical remarks and digressions occasioned by the matters they mention, lest they leave themselves [unaddressed].

And that the Qur'an comprises the books of the earlier prophets.
